en: Parivāra 9.
The Exposition on the Purpose:
For ten purposes the Tathāgata has prescribed the training rules for his disciples.
For the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of individuals who are difficult to correct,
for the ease of living of well-behaved bhikkhus, for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives,
for the inspiration of those without faith, for the increase of those with faith, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha.
What is comfortable for the Saṅgha leads to the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct.
What leads to the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct leads to the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus.
That which is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life.
That which is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.
That which is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives is for the inspiration of those who lack confidence.
That which leads to the inspiration of those without faith leads to the further increase of those with faith.
That which leads to the further increase of those with faith leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma.
That which leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma leads to the support of the Vinaya.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha is comfortable for the Saṅgha.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha is for the restraint of individuals who are difficult to correct.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus.
That which is beneficial for the Saṅgha is for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life.
That which is beneficial for the Saṅgha is for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.
That which is beneficial for the Saṅgha is for the inspiring of confidence in those who lack it.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha leads to the increase of those with faith.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha leads to the endurance of the true Dhamma.
What is beneficial for the Saṅgha leads to the support of the Vinaya.
That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct.
That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus.
That which is for the welfare of the Saṅgha is for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life.
That which is conducive to the welfare of the Saṅgha leads to the warding off of taints in future lives.
That which is conducive to the welfare of the Saṅgha leads to the inspiration of those without faith.
That which is conducive to the welfare of the Saṅgha leads to the increase of those with faith.
Whatever brings comfort to the Saṅgha serves for the endurance of the True Dhamma.
Whatever brings comfort to the Saṅgha serves for the support of the Vinaya.
Whatever brings comfort to the Saṅgha is beneficial to the Saṅgha.

That which leads to the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct … that which leads to the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus … that which leads to the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life …
That which leads to the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives;
that which leads to the inspiration of those without faith;
and that which leads to the further increase of those with faith.
That which is for the endurance of the true Dhamma...
that which is for the support of the Vinaya is beneficial to the Saṅgha.
That which is for the support of the Vinaya is comfortable for the Saṅgha.
That which is for the support of the Vinaya is for the restraint of difficult persons.
That which is for the support of the Vinaya is for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus.
That which is for the support of the Vinaya is for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life.
That which is for the benefit of the discipline is for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives.
That which is for the benefit of the discipline is for the inspiration of those without confidence.
That which is for the benefit of the discipline is for the increase of those who have confidence.
"That which is for the support of the discipline is for the endurance of the true Dhamma.
There are one hundred meanings, one hundred phenomena,
and two hundred modes of expression.
Four hundred knowledges;
the compendium on the purpose.
The compendium on the purpose is finished.
The Mahāvagga is concluded.
Its summary:
First, regarding the eight questions.
Furthermore, regarding the conditions, there are eight;
these sixteen apply to the monks and sixteen to the nuns.
The divisions within the series of recitations,
the single-increment sequence,
and the purpose of the invitation ceremony.
The compilation of the Mahāvagga is concluded.
The Section on the Purpose of the Meaning is finished.
